<reason>B won the central comparison: why the identified misconduct requires special duties rather than ordinary protections against coercion and overridden choices. A plausibly explained attachment-based exploitation and clarified its design-focused proposal, but never adequately established the remaining regulatory gap. B answered both pressure questions directly and distinguished meaningful authorization from mere disclosure; A's closing continued attacking fine-print consent instead of that stronger position.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's subscription-expiration and opted-in roleplay examples forced A to distinguish attachment from misconduct. B then targeted the unresolved boundary: payment-triggered panic is identifiable commercial pressure, while merely making departure feel cruel can also describe consensual fiction. This substantially weakened A's justification for special treatment.</best_rebuttal>
